California AB 2602 — digital replica contract provisions leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240AB2602 INDIRECT HIGH VERIFIED
California law voiding digital-replica clauses in performer contracts unless the uses are specifically described and the performer was represented — a hard limit on how Cinamate's contracts module can be drafted.

AB 2602, effective 1 January 2025, makes a contract provision unenforceable where it permits the creation and use of a digital replica of an individual's voice or likeness in place of work the individual would otherwise have performed in person, AND the provision lacks a reasonably specific description of the intended uses of the digital replica, AND the individual was not represented either by legal counsel who negotiated terms stated in a signed contract or by a union under a collective bargaining agreement addressing digital replica use. It defines a digital replica as a computer-generated, highly realistic electronic representation readily identifiable as the voice or visual likeness of an individual who did not actually perform, or whose performance was materially altered.

Key features ·  Effective 1 January 2025 · Applies to personal or professional services agreements · Requires a reasonably specific description of intended digital-replica uses · Requires either negotiating counsel or union representation for the provision to hold · Unenforceability is the remedy — the clause simply fails · Definition covers both voice and visual likeness, including materially altered performances
Pricing Not applicable — state statute.
Scale & ownership California state law; because the overwhelming majority of US film and television personal services agreements are executed under California law, it functions as a national standard.
Collides with ·  contracts / deal memos — this is the direct hit: any templated digital-replica clause Cinamate generates is void unless it names specific uses and the performer had counsel or union representation · casting — engagement paperwork is where the specificity and representation conditions must be satisfied · Studio/Local Generation — generating a performance 'in place of work the individual would otherwise have performed in person' is the exact triggering fact pattern · clearance — a void replica clause is a clearance defect that surfaces at delivery · legal exposure for a single-operator tool: an unrepresented indie performer signing a Cinamate-generated deal memo is precisely the scenario the statute targets
Stronger than Cinamate
  • It is statute, not guidance — the clause is simply unenforceable, with no cure after the fact
  • It targets exactly the low-budget, thinly-lawyered independent productions that are Cinamate's stated market, where performers are least likely to have counsel
  • A single-operator product that auto-generates deal memos is structurally likely to produce non-compliant clauses at scale
Weaker than Cinamate
  • It is satisfiable by drafting: a specific use description plus a representation acknowledgment makes the clause enforceable
  • It is a template problem, and templates are exactly what a contracts module is good at — this is a shippable fix, not an architectural one
  • It only voids the provision; it does not create statutory damages or bar the production
  • Union-covered performers are already carved in via the CBA route

EU AI Act Article 50 — transparency obligations artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/50 INDIRECT HIGH VERIFIED
Now in force as of 2 August 2026: AI systems generating synthetic video, audio or images must mark output in a machine-readable, detectable format.

Article 50 of the EU AI Act sets transparency obligations that entered into force on 2 August 2026. Providers of AI systems generating synthetic audio, image, video or text must ensure outputs are marked in a machine-readable format detectable as artificially generated or manipulated, using solutions that are effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible. Deployers must disclose when content constituting a deepfake has been artificially generated or manipulated; where the content is part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical or fictional work, the obligation is limited to disclosing the existence of such content in an appropriate manner. Disclosure must be clear and distinguishable, provided at the latest at the time of first exposure, and conform to accessibility requirements. The AI Office is facilitating codes of practice for detection and labelling.

Key features ·  In force 2 August 2026 — three weeks before this report · Machine-readable marking of synthetic audio, image, video and text required of providers · Deepfake disclosure obligation on deployers · Lighter-touch disclosure for evidently artistic, creative, satirical or fictional works — relevant to narrative film · Exception for assistive editing functions that do not substantially alter input data · Disclosure timing: at latest at first interaction or exposure · AI Office codes of practice on detection and labelling in development
Pricing Not applicable — EU regulation. Non-compliance penalties are set elsewhere in the Act and scale with turnover.
Scale & ownership Applies across the 27 EU member states and reaches non-EU providers whose output is placed on the EU market. The world's most consequential AI transparency regime to date.
Collides with ·  Studio/Local Generation — this is the provider-side obligation: Cinamate generates synthetic video and audio and must mark it machine-readably · The Cutting Room — H.264+AAC export and EDL/OTIO conform are the points where a machine-readable mark must survive; nothing in the described export pipeline carries provenance metadata · music/cue sheets — synthetic audio falls squarely inside the marking obligation · distribution deliverables — any EU delivery requires the marking to be present and intact in the master · festivals — European festivals and broadcasters will make this a submission requirement · post and vfx — transcode and grade steps are exactly where naive metadata gets stripped
Stronger than Cinamate
  • It is in force now, not pending — this is a present shipping requirement for the EU market, not a future risk
  • It bites hardest on exactly Cinamate's flagship: a system whose entire purpose is generating synthetic picture and sound
  • Compliance requires engineering in the export path (C2PA manifests or equivalent watermarking), which Cinamate's described H.264+AAC export does not do
  • Cinamate's 'private studio' positioning is in tension with a mandatory public marking regime
Weaker than Cinamate
  • The artistic/creative/fictional carve-out materially softens the deployer disclosure duty for narrative film — a film need only disclose the existence of synthetic content appropriately, not label every frame
  • Marking is required only 'as far as this is technically feasible', leaving implementation latitude
  • The obligation is satisfiable with existing open tooling (C2PA manifest signing), which is a bounded engineering task rather than a certification
  • It is a labelling duty, not a prohibition — it does not stop Cinamate selling in Europe, only ungated output

MovieLabs CSAP (Common Security Architecture for Production) movielabs.com/production-technology/production-security INDIRECT HIGH VERIFIED
The studio-authored zero-trust reference architecture for cloud production — the design standard that increasingly sits behind studio security addenda.

MovieLabs, the studios' joint technology venture, publishes the Common Security Architecture for Production, a zero-trust framework designed specifically for media creation. CSAP assumes infrastructure is already breached, requires all users, devices and services to authenticate before participating, requires mutual verification, and makes authorization policy-based. It defines three scalable security levels (100, 200, 300) so productions can match protection to content sensitivity, and is documented in five parts covering architecture description, interfaces, security levels, software-defined workflows and implementation considerations. Alongside CSAP, MovieLabs publishes Enhanced Content Protection for Production (ECPP) and Zero Trust Recommended Practices.

SOC 2 (AICPA) — Type I vs Type II www.aicpa-cima.com/topic/audit-assurance/audit-and-assurance-greater-than-soc-2 INDIRECT HIGH VERIFIED
The CPA-attested controls report that enterprise and studio procurement teams demand before onboarding a SaaS vendor, independent of any media-specific requirement.

SOC 2 is an AICPA System and Organization Controls examination performed by a licensed CPA firm on a service organization's controls. A Type I report assesses the design of controls at a single point in time. A Type II report assesses operating effectiveness over an observation window of three to twelve months, which the organization chooses. SOC 2 is not media-specific — it is the generic gate that any enterprise procurement or vendor-risk team applies, and it sits alongside TPN rather than replacing it.

Key features ·  Type I: point-in-time assessment of control design only; faster and less time-intensive · Type II: 3-12 month observation window verifying that controls actually operated effectively · Performed by an independent licensed CPA firm, not a self-assessment · Scoped against Trust Services Criteria (security is mandatory; availability, processing integrity, confidentiality and privacy are optional add-ons) · Common sequencing pattern: organizations take Type I first when deals are already blocked by missing compliance, then progress to Type II · Report is issued under NDA to customers rather than published
Pricing Not disclosed by AICPA; audit fees are negotiated per engagement with the CPA firm and vary by scope. Compliance-automation vendors that prepare organizations for the audit (Vanta, Drata) do not publish list pricing either. No verified dollar figure available.
Scale & ownership The de facto North American SaaS security standard; AICPA is the standard-setting body. Frame.io Enterprise publicly advertises being 'SOC Type 2 compliant' alongside its TPN accreditation, which indicates the pairing buyers now expect.
Collides with ·  Studio Cloud Backup — a hosted, continuously syncing production-state store is the classic in-scope system for a SOC 2 examination · The Money Room — live cost reporting, PO tracking and invoice ingestion means financial data in scope, which raises confidentiality and processing-integrity questions · finance, contracts, casting, investors — these modules hold PII, deal terms and cap-table-adjacent data that vendor-risk reviewers will ask about · workflow and projects — logical access, provisioning and deprovisioning are core Trust Services Criteria

WGA Minimum Basic Agreement — AI provisions www.wga.org/contracts/know-your-rights/artificial-intelligence INDIRECT HIGH VERIFIED
The writers' agreement establishing that AI-generated text is not literary material and cannot be assigned to a writer as source material — a direct constraint on Cinamate's writer module.

The WGA MBA's AI provisions establish that no written material produced by traditional AI or generative AI can be considered literary material. When a company provides AI-generated content to a writer, it does not count as assigned or source material, so the writer receives first-writer status and full compensation rather than a rewrite fee. Companies cannot require a writer to use AI software when performing writing services, though voluntary use may be permitted under company policy. Studios must disclose to writers when materials incorporate AI-generated content. AI-generated material cannot disqualify a writer from separated rights or affect credit determinations. The Guild asserts that exploiting writers' material to train AI is prohibited by the MBA or other law.

Key features ·  AI/GAI output is not 'literary material' under the MBA · AI-generated material handed to a writer is not assigned or source material — the writer is a first writer, paid accordingly · Companies cannot compel a writer to use AI tools · Mandatory disclosure to the writer when supplied material contains AI-generated content · AI material cannot affect writing credit or separated rights · Guild position that training on writers' material is prohibited · A 2026 MBA is referenced on the WGA contracts page, indicating the agreement has been renegotiated since the 2023 terms
Pricing Not applicable — collective bargaining agreement with published minimums.
Scale & ownership WGA West and WGA East together cover essentially all US screen and television writing on signatory productions. The 2023 MBA followed a 148-day strike in which AI was a central issue.
Collides with ·  writer — this is the direct collision: a module that generates or develops screenplay material runs straight into the disclosure and first-writer rules · boards (storyboards/animatics) — derivative generation from AI-written material inherits the disclosure obligation · contracts / deal memos — writer agreements on signatory productions must reflect AI disclosure and cannot mandate AI use · clearance and distribution — chain of title for the screenplay is the foundation of the whole package · projects and workflow — provenance tracking of which text was AI-generated becomes a contractual record-keeping requirement
Stronger than Cinamate
  • It is binding on every signatory production and enforced through arbitration
  • The economics are inverted against AI use: handing a writer AI-generated material makes them a first writer at full rate, removing the cost saving that would justify it
  • The Guild's stated position against training on writers' work creates exposure for any tool whose model provenance is undisclosed — Cinamate discloses nothing about its generation models
Weaker than Cinamate
  • It regulates the employment relationship, not the tool — a producer using Cinamate privately without engaging a WGA writer is outside its reach
  • It explicitly permits voluntary writer use of AI with an appropriate policy, so Cinamate's writer module is usable on covered productions with disclosure
  • Non-signatory independent production, Cinamate's stated market, is largely unaffected
  • Disclosure is a feature Cinamate could ship — an AI-provenance flag per scene would satisfy it and differentiate the writer module

Nonprofit certification that a generative AI model was trained only on licensed data — the emerging trust mark for AI tools selling into rights-sensitive industries.

Fairly Trained certifies generative AI companies that license their training data rather than using copyrighted work without consent. Its stated mission is to make sure the human creators behind training data are treated fairly, and it certifies AI companies that do not use any copyrighted work without a license. For a film-industry buyer, the certification answers the question that increasingly precedes any AI-tool purchase: what was this model trained on, and can using it create exposure for my production.

NO FAKES Act (S.1367, 119th Congress) www.govinfo.gov/app/details/BILLS-119s1367is INDIRECT MEDIUM VERIFIED
The proposed federal digital-replica right — still in committee, but the bill that would federalize what California AB 2602 and AB 1836 do today.

S.1367, the Nurture Originals, Foster Art, and Keep Entertainment Safe Act of 2025, is a bill to protect intellectual property rights in the voice and visual likeness of individuals. It was introduced 9 April 2025 by Senator Christopher Coons (D-DE) with cosponsors Marsha Blackburn (R-TN), Amy Klobuchar (D-MN) and Thom Tillis (R-NC), and was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on the Judiciary. The introduced-bill record shows no legislative activity beyond that referral. It would create a federal property-style right in voice and likeness, addressing the patchwork the Copyright Office's Part 1 report recommended fixing.

§22 Gap Fill — Players & Categories the First Sweep Missed ⟦S22⟧

Market read · METHOD CAVEAT: this session's WebSearch budget (200/200) was already exhausted before I began, so every entry above was verified by direct WebFetch on the vendor's own page. Several targets were unreachable to automated fetch and are therefore NOT listed despite being real: Backstage, ProductionHUB, IMDbPro, OOONA, Metaphysic, ActionVFX, Pond5, Fab and QTAKE all returned 403/429/503. Those remain unfilled gaps, not non-existent ones. WHOLE CATEGORIES THE ROSTER MISSED. Insurance and completion bonds (Film Finances, Front Row, Athos) — E&O is a hard gate on distribution and the roster has zero entries. Casting marketplaces — the roster names Breakdown Services but omits Talent Systems, which owns Casting Networks, Spotlight, Casting Frontier, Tagmin and Staff Me Up, with 2M+ talent profiles; this is the largest single omission. Crew marketplaces (Staff Me Up 489K crew; ProductionHUB unreachable). Location marketplaces (Giggster, Peerspace, SetScouter — the roster's locations coverage is empty despite Cinamate claiming a permit DB). Equipment rental/asset tracking (Rentman, Cheqroom at $184/admin/month — verified but trimmed for length). Script supervision and continuity (ScriptE Systems, with iPad apps in exactly the on-set mobile space Cinamate concedes). Virtual production and LED volumes (disguise's 402 studios in 116 countries, Aximmetry's free tier, Pixotope, Mo-Sys — all verified, an entire production paradigm absent). On-set/DIT and dailies origination (Assimilate SCRATCH, Teradek camera control for ARRI/RED/Sony). MAM and archive at indie price (axle ai at $20/TB/month). Localization and captioning (ZOO Digital plc, Simon Says, Subtitle Edit). Theatrical mastering/DCP (DCP-o-matic free, easyDCP/Fraunhofer, Qube Cinema). Revenue collection and CAM (FilmChain) — the roster models waterfalls but never names anyone who runs one. Crowdfunding (Seed&Spark, $96.4M raised, 82% funded). Music clearance software (Trevanna Tracks, with Netflix/Apple/HBO/WBD/Paramount). Post-facility resource scheduling (freispace, FoxOMS/Sonderplan). Editorial interchange standards (OpenTimelineIO — Cinamate markets "OTIO conform" as a differentiator when OTIO is free, Apache-2.0 and Academy-governed). World models (Odyssey $310M Series B, Decart $3.1B) — a 2026 architectural shift absent from a roster otherwise dense with generative video. AI-filmmaking education (Curious Refuge, 172+ countries — and it sits inside Promise Studios, which the roster lists separately without noticing the link). GEOGRAPHY. Coverage is US/UK/EU-skewed. Verified non-US additions here: Rentman (NL), Aximmetry (HU), Mo-Sys (UK), Dalet (FR), ZOO Digital plc (UK, with India/Spain/Korea facilities), freispace (DE), FoxOMS/Sonderplan (AU), SetScouter (CA), Qube Cinema (IN), FilmChain (UK/EU Horizon 2020). Still genuinely unfilled: Nollywood/Africa, LATAM, Japan, mainland-China production management, Middle East. Movibeta (the Spanish/LATAM festival platform) and lina.film both failed to return usable content — the latter's DNS does not resolve, so treat the AlternativeTo listing of "Lína" as stale. ROSTER ENTRIES THAT LOOK WRONG OR SUSPICIOUS. (1) Duplication is pervasive and internally contradictory: Filmustage appears in four sections at $99/mo (Capterra) in one and $55/mo in another (resolved: the vendor page shows $79/mo); StudioBinder appears three times with Starter at $29 and also $42, Professional at $99 and also $127; Movie Magic Budgeting is $42.99/mo in one section and $24.99/mo-billed-annually in another; Saturation Pro is $25/mo in one and $32/mo in another; Studiovity appears three times with three incompatible price sets ($3/mo, $18/user/yr, $24/user/mo); Cinetech is "not disclosed" in one section and $49/mo in another; FinalBit is "not verified," then $15-$75, then $40/$100. Roughly 30 vendors are duplicated. (2) Relationship coding is inconsistent for the same vendor: Movie Magic is "indirect" in one section and "direct/critical" in another; Cinelytic is "indirect" in finance and "direct/critical" in analytics; Filmustage swings direct/adjacent. (3) Vitrina AI appears twice with irreconcilable scale claims — 140,000 companies / 400,000 projects versus 300,000+ / 1.6M+; one is stale. (4) The three Autodesk "Flow" products are conflated: Flow Capture is described as "formerly Moxion and PIX" in the security section while PIX is listed as a separate entry in the post section — both framings cannot be right. (5) Cinemata (cinemata.ru) is a name collision risk: cinemata.org is an established, unrelated EngageMedia social-issue film platform for Asia-Pacific; the .ru entry has no company, no pricing page and a sign-in wall, and should be treated as possible vaporware rather than a competitor. (6) Beemer (beemerdocs.com) is a startup pitch-deck tool with no film footprint and should be removed. (7) Lore Machine (NXDOMAIN) and "Plot (plotstoryboards)" (no live site) are dead entries. (8) Cine Tracer's own domain now serves an apartment-rental site — correctly flagged, but it belongs in a "dead" bucket, not a competitor list. (9) One further dead-vendor signal the roster missed: sonyci.com/pricing now 302-redirects to a parked tracking page at ww1.sonyci.com, suggesting Sony Ci Media Cloud — formerly a significant camera-to-cloud, review and archive player — has gone dark. (10) Wrapal is named in the task brief as a location marketplace but appears nowhere in the roster; it has in fact been acquired by SetScouter, with wrapal.com 301-redirecting. WHAT THIS MEANS FOR CINAMATE. The roster over-indexes on the two categories where Cinamate looks strongest (generative video, AI pre-production) and under-indexes on the categories that decide whether a finished film can be delivered, insured, cleared, cast, crewed, localised, projected or paid out. Cinamate's 28 modules assert coverage of casting, locations, wardrobe, props, safety, music cue sheets and distribution deliverables; in every one of those, an entrenched specialist with named studio customers already exists and was absent from the analysis. The single most under-weighted structural risk is not a rival AI studio — it is that a Cinamate-produced film still needs an E&O policy, a DCP, a cue sheet a distributor accepts, localised subtitles, and a collection account, and Cinamate touches none of those chains.
Odyssey odyssey.ml DIRECT HIGH VERIFIED
A $310M Series B world-model lab shipping real-time, minutes-long interactive video — a category the entire roster missed, and a direct threat to the premise that film is generated as fixed clips.

Odyssey is an AI lab "pioneering general world models: causal, multimodal systems that learn to understand and simulate the world." Its flagship Odyssey-2 generates interactive video simulations minutes in length from an image or text prompt, streaming in real time rather than producing fixed clips. Starchild-1 is a multimodal world model learning from richer interaction than visual observation alone; Agora-1 is a multi-agent simulator allowing several participants inside one shared simulation; PROWL-1 is a reinforcement-learning framework using adversarial exploration to improve world-model performance. The strategic threat to Cinamate is architectural: if generated footage becomes an interactive, directable, real-time stream, the fixed script-to-render pipeline Cinamate is built around becomes the wrong shape.

Key features ·  Odyssey-2 — real-time interactive video streams, minutes in length, from image or text prompt · Starchild-1 — multimodal world model beyond visual observation · Agora-1 — multi-agent shared simulation · PROWL-1 — adversarial-exploration RL framework for world models · Publicly available for testing while still early-stage
Pricing Not disclosed. Odyssey-2 is publicly available for testing; no subscription, credit or per-generation pricing is published on the site.

DCP-o-matic is "a program to generate DCPs (digital cinema packages)" released under GPL-2.0, with active development branches for the v2.18.x and v2.19.x lines. A DCP is the mandatory deliverable for any theatrical or most festival screenings; without one a finished film cannot be projected in a cinema. DCP-o-matic makes that step free, which is a meaningful hole in Cinamate's distribution-deliverables and festivals story — a producer who has made a film in Cinamate still needs a DCP, and the standard answer is this open-source tool rather than a paid module.

The virtual production and LED-volume platform behind 402 VP/xR studios in 116 countries — the whole category of on-stage real-time production the roster omitted.

disguise is an integrated software, hardware and services platform for real-time visual production: LED volumes, extended reality stages, projection mapping and live events. Software includes Designer (cloud-based design), disguise X1, RenderStream (graphics control) and Mapping Matter; hardware spans the EX, VX, GX and RX media server ranges plus Omnical calibration and VFC video format conversion cards. It partners with Epic Games and Nvidia. This is where in-camera VFX actually gets shot — the alternative path to "generate the image" that Cinamate's Studio/Local Generation flagship never engages with.

Key features ·  Designer — cloud-based real-time show design · RenderStream graphics control engine for LED volumes and xR · Mapping Matter projection mapping · EX/VX/GX/RX media server hardware ranges · Omnical camera/projector calibration · VFC video format conversion cards · Epic Games and Nvidia technology partnerships
Pricing Not published. The site references "Designer Pricing Plans" and links a financing solutions page but discloses no figures; hardware and licences are quoted.
Scale & ownership Claims 80% of the world's biggest A-list live tours and 90% of Tier 1 live shows run on the disguise platform; 402 VP and xR studios; operations in 116 countries. Partners named include Epic Games, Nvidia, Warner Bros. and ROE Visual. Funding and ownership not disclosed on the pages reviewed.
Collides with ·  studio/local generation · sets · vfx · production · tools
Stronger than Cinamate
  • 402 real virtual-production stages worldwide versus Cinamate's claimed 36 verified stage facilities as a database entry
  • Produces in-camera final-pixel imagery that is unambiguously ownable and union-compatible — a legal posture generative output does not have
  • Deep hardware/software integration with Epic and Nvidia
  • Genuine global footprint across 116 countries
Weaker than Cinamate
  • Capital-intensive: requires a stage, LED wall, media servers and a crew — the opposite of single-operator
  • No pricing transparency
  • Nothing upstream (script, breakdown, budget) or downstream (edit, distribution, festivals)
  • Broadcast/live-events revenue skew rather than narrative film
https://www.disguise.one/en
Front Row Insurance Brokers www.frontrowinsurance.com INDIRECT LOW VERIFIED
Specialist entertainment broker with Producer's E&O, DICE annual policies and short-shoot cover across Canada and Los Angeles.

Front Row is a specialist entertainment insurance brokerage covering film, music, theatre and photography, with offices in Vancouver, Calgary, Toronto, Montreal, Halifax and Los Angeles. Its film and TV line includes production packages, Producer's E&O, Short Shoot Insurance, annual DICE (Documentary/Industrial/Commercial/Educational) producers' insurance, studio art services insurance, a documentary programme and film equipment rental house insurance. It sits directly on the compliance path between Cinamate's clearance/contracts output and a distributor accepting delivery.

Key features ·  Producer's Errors & Omissions policies · Production package insurance · Short Shoot Insurance for micro-productions · Annual DICE producers' insurance · Documentary-specific programme · Film equipment rental house insurance · Six offices across Canada plus Los Angeles
Pricing Not disclosed. No published prices or minimum premiums; quotes are requested through the site or a local office.

Stronger than Cinamate
  • Regional depth in Canada, a major production territory Cinamate's 21-jurisdiction tax-credit module implicitly targets
  • Owns the E&O relationship that converts a clearance report into an insurable, deliverable film

Weaker than Cinamate
  • No published pricing at all
  • No software product, no automation

OpenTimelineIO (Academy Software Foundation) github.com/AcademySoftwareFoundation/OpenTimelineIO INDIRECT LOW VERIFIED
The Apache-2.0 editorial interchange standard Cinamate's own "EDL/OTIO conform" claim depends on — owned by the Academy, not by any vendor.

OpenTimelineIO is "an interchange format and API for editorial cut information" — cut order, lengths and external media references, deliberately not a media container. It is maintained by the Academy Software Foundation under Apache 2.0. Adapters in sibling repositories provide interoperability with Final Cut Pro XML, AAF, CMX 3600 EDL and other formats, and the Python bindings support Media Linkers, HookScripts and custom SchemaDefs. Cinamate advertises "EDL/OTIO conform" as a differentiator; OTIO is in fact a free, neutral, industry-governed standard that every competitor can and does implement.

Key features ·  Native .otio, .otioz and .otiod formats · Adapters for FCP XML, AAF and CMX 3600 EDL · Media Linker, HookScript and SchemaDef plugin types · Python bindings; VFX Platform 2022-2025, Python 3.9-3.12 · Apache 2.0 licence, Academy Software Foundation governance
Pricing Free. Apache 2.0 licence — unrestricted commercial use, no revenue threshold.
Scale & ownership 2,000+ GitHub stars, 342 forks, 99 watchers. Maintained by the Academy Software Foundation (the Linux Foundation/AMPAS joint body), with the codebase originating at Pixar. No company, no funding — industry-governed infrastructure.
Collides with ·  editor (The Cutting Room) · post · vfx · workflow · dailies
Stronger than Cinamate
  • Academy-governed neutral standard — vendor-independent credibility Cinamate cannot claim for itself
  • Free and Apache 2.0, so OTIO conform is table stakes, not a differentiator
  • Broad adapter ecosystem covering AAF, FCPXML and EDL that a from-scratch implementation must match edge-case for edge-case
  • Actively maintained against the VFX Reference Platform
Weaker than Cinamate
  • A library and format, not a product — no UI, no workflow, no user-facing value on its own
  • Requires engineering to use
  • Notably, AAF adapter support is a separate repo and historically the hardest conform path to get right
https://github.com/AcademySoftwareFoundation/OpenTimelineIO
Peerspace www.peerspace.com INDIRECT LOW VERIFIED
The global venue marketplace filmmakers actually book through — film shoot, video shoot and music video are first-class booking categories across LA, NY, London, Paris, Berlin, Sydney and Barcelona.

Peerspace connects property owners with people booking spaces by the hour, with production explicitly among its core use cases: photo shoot, video shoot, music video and film shoot are named activity types. Inventory spans "professionally equipped studios to unconventional rooms and residences." For an independent producer it is the practical substitute for a location scout and for a location database — you search, you see the price, you book it.

Key features ·  Hourly venue booking with production-specific activity filters · Studios, residences and unconventional interiors · Global city coverage (London, Vancouver, Paris, Sydney, New York, Los Angeles, Berlin, Barcelona) · Host/guest messaging and in-platform booking · "Made in Peerspace" project gallery and annual Open Door Awards (2026 edition running)
Pricing Not disclosed on the pages reviewed. Peerspace publishes no host or guest fee percentage on its homepage; individual listings carry hourly rates set by hosts.
Scale & ownership No quantitative listing, user or GMV figures published on the homepage. Operates across major North American, European and Australian cities. Funding and ownership not disclosed on the pages reviewed.
Collides with ·  locations · sets · production
Stronger than Cinamate
  • Genuinely international inventory including EU and Australia, well beyond Cinamate's claimed 36 stage facilities and 6 permit hubs
  • Zero learning curve and no invite required
  • Prices visible before you commit
Weaker than Cinamate
  • No permit workflow, no location release paperwork
  • No fee transparency
  • Not film-specific — production competes with parties and offsites for the same inventory
  • No connection to schedule, budget or breakdown
https://www.peerspace.com/
Seed&Spark www.seedandspark.com INDIRECT LOW VERIFIED
The film-specific crowdfunding platform with an 82% success rate and $96.4M raised across 8,071 projects — the way independent films actually get financed at the level Cinamate targets.

Seed&Spark is a crowdfunding platform where "creators and audiences work together to bring incredible new projects to life," specialising in film and storytelling. Filmmakers launch campaigns, and the platform runs themed "Rallies" — large multi-project initiatives with partner prizes — plus a crowdfunding playbook and creator events. It requires an inclusion statement from every creator. For the independent producer Cinamate targets, this is the realistic alternative to the investors module: not modelling an equity waterfall, but raising the money from an audience.

Key features ·  Film-specific crowdfunding campaigns · Rallies — themed multi-project funding drives with partner prizes · Crowdfunding playbook and creator education · Inclusion statement requirement for all creators · Audience-building tools alongside fundraising
Pricing Not disclosed on the homepage. Seed&Spark publishes no platform fee or commission rate on the pages reviewed — treat any percentage as unverified.
Scale & ownership Self-reported: 82% of projects funded, $96,376,230 raised in total, 8,071 projects created. Also states roughly 80% of crowdfunding dollars go to local wages and 82% of projects include women in key roles. Funding, ownership and headcount not disclosed on the pages reviewed.
Collides with ·  investors · finance · distribution · festivals
Stronger than Cinamate
  • An 82% funded rate and $96M raised is verifiable outcome data; Cinamate's 3,708-film model with a 15.5% failure rate is a forecast, not a track record
  • Reaches the money source most sub-$1M independent films actually use
  • Audience-building is a distribution asset the film keeps after the raise
  • Publishes real aggregate outcome statistics
Weaker than Cinamate
  • No fee disclosure
  • Not software for making a film — purely fundraising
  • Ceiling is low: crowdfunding rarely finances a full feature budget
  • No forecasting, budgeting or waterfall modelling
https://www.seedandspark.com/
Subtitle Edit (open source) github.com/SubtitleEdit/subtitleedit INDIRECT LOW VERIFIED
The free MIT-licensed subtitle editor with 13.9k GitHub stars, offline-first, running on Windows, macOS and Linux — the zero-cost floor under every captioning deliverable.

Subtitle Edit is an open-source desktop subtitle editor for creating, syncing, converting and editing subtitle files. It handles editing, format conversion, video playback and local auto-backup entirely offline on the user's own machine. It supports optional integrations with third-party translation, speech-to-text, text-to-speech, OCR and dictionary services — meaning a producer can run local Whisper-class ASR through it at zero marginal cost, which is exactly the local-GPU economics Cinamate markets.

Key features ·  Subtitle editing, syncing and format conversion · Integrated video playback · Local auto-backup, offline-first, no telemetry on subtitle or media content · Optional speech-to-text, TTS, translation, OCR and dictionary providers · Windows, macOS and Linux builds · MIT licence
Pricing Free. MIT licence. Cost is the operator's own compute only.
Scale & ownership 13.9k GitHub stars, 27,069 commits, 223 open issues — a long-running, actively maintained community project with no company behind it. Cross-platform releases distributed via GitHub.
Collides with ·  distribution deliverables · post · editor · screening
Stronger than Cinamate
  • Free and MIT-licensed — no revenue threshold, no per-seat cost, no invite
  • Runs fully offline with an explicit no-data-collection posture, a stronger privacy story than a 4-minute cloud sync
  • Cross-platform including Linux
  • 27,000 commits of maturity in a format-compatibility problem that is all edge cases
Weaker than Cinamate
  • Subtitles only — no production, post, generation or business capability
  • Desktop app with a dated interface and a real learning curve
  • No support contract, no SLA, no security certification
https://github.com/SubtitleEdit/subtitleedit
Teradek (Videndum) teradek.com INDIRECT LOW LIKELY
The on-set wireless video, streaming and camera-control hardware layer — including direct ARRI, RED and Sony camera control — that explains exactly what LightsKiddo's integrations mean and Cinamate's do not.

Teradek makes wireless video transmission, encoding/decoding and camera-control hardware for professional production: the Bolt 6 and Ace 750 zero-delay wireless monitoring systems; Serv and Link AX for production streaming; the Prism encoder/decoder family (Jetpack, Flex, Mobile, Rack); Teradek RT wireless lens control with CTRL.5 offering "Sony, RED® and ARRI® Camera Control" over WiFi or Ethernet; and Link/Data/Node multi-WAN modems. This is the physical substrate of camera-to-cloud dailies, and it is the concrete form of the integration advantage the brief attributes to LightsKiddo.

Key features ·  Bolt 6 / Ace 750 zero-delay wireless video monitoring · Prism Jetpack / Flex / Mobile / Rack encoders and decoders · Serv Series and Link AX production streaming · Teradek RT wireless lens control; CTRL.5 camera control for Sony, RED and ARRI · Link / Data / Node multi-WAN bonded modems
Pricing Not disclosed on the homepage. Sold as hardware through dealers; treat any figure as unverified.
Scale & ownership Careers links on the site reference Videndum, indicating Teradek sits within the Videndum plc group (Creative Solutions division) — treat the ownership as likely rather than confirmed from this page. Revenue and unit volumes not disclosed.
Collides with ·  dailies · tools · production · today · screening
Stronger than Cinamate
  • Native camera control for the three camera systems that shoot most professional narrative work — the precise integration class Cinamate lacks
  • Hardware on set works with no internet, no GPU and no sync interval
  • Bonded cellular uplink makes true real-time transport possible, versus Cinamate's 4-minute sync
Weaker than Cinamate
  • Hardware capex, not software; no workflow, planning or post capability
  • No published pricing
  • Irrelevant to a production that never points a camera at anything
https://teradek.com/
⟦S23⟧

§23 Appendix A — The Fact-Check Ledger

An adversarial verification agent re-tested the ~36 riskiest claims produced by the research sweep against primary sources (vendor pricing pages, filings, registries, live DNS/HTTP probes). Its verdicts are reproduced here in full; every refuted claim was corrected in the catalog before publication, and every unverifiable claim is labeled at point of use. This ledger is included so the reader can see not only what this report asserts, but what it declined to assert.

REFUTED  Cinetech
Claim: Cinetech pricing is 'Not disclosed on the site. No published tiers.'
Finding: Cinetech publishes full pricing: Solo Creator $49/month (500 bonus + 250 credits/mo at $0.02/credit, 100GB), Team $149/month for 5 members (+$25/member, 1TB pooled), Pay As You Go at $0.08/credit, Studio custom. The roster's other Cinetech entry has these figures right; the 'not disclosed' entry is simply wrong.
https://www.cinetech.ai/pricing
REFUTED  ComfyUI / Comfy Cloud
Claim: Comfy Cloud costs Standard $16/mo, Creator $28/mo, Pro $80/mo, Team $630/mo.
Finding: Those are annual-billing monthly equivalents presented as monthly prices. Month-to-month rates are Standard $20, Creator $35, Pro $100, Team $700. The annual totals in the roster ($192/$336/$960/$7,560) and the credit allocations (4,200/7,400/21,100/147,700) are correct, as is the free desktop app.
https://www.comfy.org/pricing
REFUTED  Filmustage
Claim: Filmustage Director's Cut costs $55/month (or $660/year), stated in three separate roster sections as verified from filmustage.com/pricing.
Finding: Director's Cut is $79/month, not $55. The $660/year annual figure and the 1,700 coins/cycle are correct, and $660 is a ~30% saving off $79x12=$948 — which is arithmetically impossible against a $55 monthly rate. The $55 number appears nowhere on the vendor page.
https://filmustage.com/pricing/
REFUTED  Google Flow (Veo 4 / DeepMind)
Claim: Google Flow was relaunched in February 2026 as a unified idea-to-finished-video pipeline running on Veo 4.
Finding: There is no Veo 4. Google's own Flow page names Veo 3.1 as the current model and mentions no Veo 4 anywhere. The roster contradicts itself: a later section correctly lists 'Google Veo 3.1 + Flow'. Flow's published plans are confirmed exactly (Free 50 daily credits; Google AI Plus $4.99/mo 200 credits; AI Pro $19.99/mo 1,000; AI Ultra $99.99-$199.99/mo 10,000-25,000).
https://labs.google/flow/about
REFUTED  Katalist
Claim: Katalist is priced from $29 to $399/month: Essential $29, Pro $79 (unlimited image generation), Business $399, plus enterprise.
Finding: Katalist's published tiers are Essential $19/mo, Pro $39/mo, Unlimited $99/mo (2 seats), Enterprise custom; annual equivalents $348/$374/$948 per year. There is no $399 Business tier. The roster lists Katalist twice with mutually contradictory prices — the storyboards-section entry ($19/$39/$99) is the correct one.
https://www.katalist.ai/pricing
REFUTED  Open-Sora (HPC-AI Tech)
Claim: Open-Sora's last major release was March 2025, leaving it well behind the current open frontier.
Finding: The repository was last pushed 9 April 2026 and has 29,293 stars — it is not a March-2025-dormant project. The Apache-2.0 license is confirmed. By contrast, the roster's dormancy calls on Replica Studios, Lore Machine and Cine Tracer all check out.
https://github.com/hpcaitech/Open-Sora
REFUTED  Saturation.io
Claim: Saturation.io paid plans start at $25/month.
Finding: Saturation's entry paid plan is Pro at $32/month ($384/year); Team is $79/month ($948/year); Creator is free. The roster's own later entries state $32 correctly — the '$25/month' figure in the AI-breakdown section is wrong.
https://saturation.io/pricing
REFUTED  Slated
Claim: Slated pricing is 'Not disclosed in sources I verified. Historically a mix of submission/analysis fees and success-based participation; treat specifics as unverified.'
Finding: Slated publishes a full rate card: Active Project Listing $34.99/month, Script Analysis $495, Financial Analysis $495, Script+Financial bundle $795, EP Consulting $595/month, individual membership and opportunity matching free. The roster's distribution-section entry has these right; the finance-section entry claiming non-disclosure is wrong.
https://get.slated.com/pricing
UNVERIFIABLE  Celtx (Backlight)
Claim: Celtx pricing is Writer $11.24/month, Writer Pro $18.74/month, Team from $67.49/month billed yearly.
Finding: Celtx's own pricing page shows tier names, seat and project limits and a '25% off yearly' banner but no dollar figures at all. The roster is honest about this in two entries and then presents the same third-party numbers as fact in a third. Treat all Celtx dollar amounts as third-party estimates, not vendor-published.
https://www.celtx.com/pricing/
UNVERIFIABLE  Filmhub
Claim: Filmhub puts titles onto 130+ streaming channels across 200+ territories, on plans of Core $0, Plus $999/yr and Pro $1,999/yr with an 80/20 split.
Finding: filmhub.com/pricing and /plans both 404. The homepage says Filmhub works with 'over 100 of the world's biggest exhibitors' — not 130+ channels — and publishes no revenue split and no plan prices. The $999/$1,999 tiers and the 80/20 figure could not be confirmed from the vendor.
https://filmhub.com/
UNVERIFIABLE  FinalBit / Nolan AI
Claim: FinalBit (formerly Nolan AI) charges Creator $40/month and Pro $100/month, with promo codes bringing them to $28/$70.
Finding: The rebrand is real and verifiable — nolanai.app/pricing 301-redirects to finalbitai.com/pricing. But no dollar figures render on the pricing page to a fetcher. The roster gives three mutually inconsistent accounts of FinalBit pricing across three sections ($40/$100; 'could not be confirmed, trackers say $15-$75'; 'not disclosed in retrievable form'). No FinalBit price should be cited.
https://www.finalbitai.com/pricing
UNVERIFIABLE  Higgsfield AI
Claim: Higgsfield raised a $400M Series B led by DST Global at a $5.4B valuation on 17 August 2026, with $700M annualized revenue, 30M users, 390 of the Fortune 500, and a 110-minute AI feature made for $2M in four weeks.
Finding: None of it could be confirmed. Higgsfield's own pricing page returns no plan data to a fetcher, and no primary source for the round, valuation, revenue or user figures was reachable. This is the single largest cluster of unsourced numbers in the roster — a $5.4B valuation and $700M ARR for a company eight months out from a claimed $1.3B mark should not be repeated without a named filing or press release. The roster itself admits the pricing tiers come from third-party trackers.
https://higgsfield.ai/pricing
UNVERIFIABLE  Movie Magic Budgeting (Entertainment Partners)
Claim: Movie Magic Budgeting costs $42.99/month, stated as $515.88/year, with ~40% saving on an annual subscription.
Finding: EP publishes no price on the Movie Magic Budgeting product page — it routes to 'Get pricing', and the EP store returned HTTP 503. The claim is also internally incoherent: $42.99 x 12 = $515.88 exactly, so the quoted 'annual' price is just twelve monthly payments and cannot simultaneously represent a 40% discount. A separate roster entry gives $24.99/month billed annually ($299.88/year) for the same product. At most one of these can be right; neither is verified.
https://www.ep.com/movie-magic-budgeting/
UNVERIFIABLE  Movie Magic Scheduling (Entertainment Partners)
Claim: Movie Magic Scheduling is $29.99/month introductory (list $39.99) and $199.88/year introductory (list $279.88), 'Verified on EP Store (Aug 2026)'.
Finding: The EP product page publishes no prices and the EP store was unreachable (HTTP 503). The 'verified' label is not supportable. The related claim that Movie Magic Scheduling 6 ends sale/support mid-2026 and that version 10 is current also could not be confirmed from EP's own pages.
https://www.ep.com/movie-magic-scheduling/
UNVERIFIABLE  Netflix / InterPositive
Claim: Netflix bought Ben Affleck's stealth AI post-production startup InterPositive for $587M in cash, a 16-person team, price revealed in a July 2026 filing.
Finding: The acquisition itself is confirmed — Netflix's newsroom announced it on 5 March 2026, with Affleck joining as Senior Advisor. But the announcement discloses no price and no team size. The $587M figure, the 16-person headcount, the July 2026 filing and the 'will not commercialize' commitment could not be confirmed from any primary source; treat the dollar figure as unsupported.
https://about.netflix.com/en/news/why-interpositive-is-joining-netflix
UNVERIFIABLE  Runway
Claim: Runway raised a $315M Series E at a $5.3B post-money valuation in February 2026 led by General Atlantic, with ~$860M raised across 7 rounds and ~$300M annualized revenue.
Finding: No primary source confirms a 2026 Series E. Runway's documented rounds total roughly $545M ($2M seed, $8.5M A, $35M B, $50M C at $500M, $141M C-extension at $1.5B led by Google/Nvidia/Salesforce, and $308M in April 2025 at over $3B led by General Atlantic). The roster's claim looks like a drifted restatement of the April 2025 General Atlantic round; the $5.3B valuation, February 2026 date and ~$860M total are unsupported. Runway's consumer pricing IS confirmed exactly: Free $0/125 credits, Standard $12, Pro $28, Max $76 (annual billing).
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runway_(company)
UNVERIFIABLE  TPN (Trusted Partner Network)
Claim: TPN annual membership runs on a published revenue-banded schedule from $250 (self-employed) to $85K ($200M+), with $500 assessor accreditation valid two years.
Finding: ttpn.org returned no content to repeated fetches (membership, pricing and root pages all came back empty). The fee schedule, the Shield tier rebrand and the SSP-to-TPX rename could not be confirmed against any primary source. The MPA ownership of TPN is well established but was not verified here either.
https://www.ttpn.org/membership/

CONFIRMED  StudioBinder
Claim: StudioBinder claims more than 1.5 million production companies and brands worldwide rely on the platform.
Finding: Confirmed as a verbatim vendor claim on studiobinder.com. Treat it as marketing, not a verified user count — 1.5 million production companies exceeds any plausible global count of production companies, and StudioBinder is estimated at roughly 21-29 employees and ~$2.3M revenue. Separately, StudioBinder's pricing page 301s to app.studiobinder.com and renders no figures, so the $29/$49/$99 'support-page ladder' could not be confirmed.
